title: Smooth compact perturbations preserve the determinant integral difference

content.display_title: Smooth compact perturbations preserve the determinant integral difference
content.one_sentence_role: Builds a finite telescope from single-output perturbations with compactly supported fluxes.
content.natural_language_statement:
Fix $n\geq1$ and let $g,u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^\infty$, with $u$ compactly supported. Then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\bigl(\det D(g+u)(x)-\det Dg(x)\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
content.assumptions: Both maps are smooth of all finite orders, as stated in the exact theorem. Only $u$ must have compact support. No decay or global integrability is assumed for $g$ or for its determinant separately. Here and below $g_j(x):=(g(x))_j$ and $u_j(x):=(u(x))_j$ are scalar coordinate maps. Compact support means that $\operatorname{supp}u:=\overline{\{x:u(x)\ne0\}}$ is compact.
content.conclusion: The determinant difference is integrable and has integral zero. This statement is an integral of a difference; it does not assert equality of two separately integrable whole-space determinants.
content.proof_summary: Add the components of $u$ one at a time, prove each determinant increment integrable with zero integral, and add the finitely many increments.

proof_steps.text:
For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, define the smooth hybrid map by its coordinates:
$$(g_S(x))_j=\begin{cases}g_j(x)+u_j(x),&j\in S,\\g_j(x),&j\notin S.\end{cases}$$
Then $g_\varnothing=g$, $g_{\{1,\ldots,n\}}=g+u$, and for $i\notin S$,
$$g_{S\cup\{i\}}(x)=g_S(x)+u_i(x)e_i.$$
Each scalar coordinate $u_i$ is smooth and has compact support, since
$$\{x:u_i(x)\ne0\}\subseteq\{x:u(x)\ne0\}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{supp}u_i\subseteq\operatorname{supp}u.$$

Apply the component-flux identity with base $g_S$, scalar $u_i$, and row $i$. Smoothness supplies the required $C^2$ and $C^1$ hypotheses. The flux $u_i C_i(Dg_S)$ is $C^1$ and compactly supported because its support is contained in that of $u_i$. The compact-support divergence theorem gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\bigl(\det Dg_{S\cup\{i\}}-\det Dg_S\bigr)=0.$$
This increment is integrable: it is continuous and vanishes outside the compact support of $u_i$, since there $u_i$ is locally zero and its derivative is zero.

Choose any ordering of the $n$ coordinates and write its successive subsets as $S_0,\ldots,S_n$. Pointwise telescoping gives
$$\det D(g+u)-\det Dg=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\det Dg_{S_{r+1}}-\det Dg_{S_r}\bigr).$$
Every summand is integrable by the preceding step. Linearity of the integral is therefore legitimate for this finite sum, and its integral is the sum of $n$ zeros. No splitting into the two unrestricted determinant integrals is used.

content.lean_realization_notes: The one-coordinate integral lemma needs only a $C^2$ base map and a $C^1$ compactly supported scalar perturbation. The theorem here retains its stronger stated $C^\infty$ hypotheses and applies that lemma to each smooth hybrid.
